sources.title: Frequently asked questions on stocking densities
Nên nuôi bao nhiêu cá trong bể thủy sinh?
Cách Tính Mật Độ Nuôi Cá Cảnh Để Cá Luôn Khỏe Mạnh
Q&A: How to Keep Your Fish Tank Safe During a Power Outage

facts.fact: Stocking densities are only a rough guide and an oversimplification; they break down once large fish, which put more load on the filter, are in the mix.
Recommended density for tropical freshwater and coldwater tanks: 1 inch of fish per gallon (2.5 cm per 4.55 L).
Pond guideline: 10 inches of fish per 100 gallons (25 cm per 455 L).
Vietnamese hobby guideline: 1 cm of fish per 1.5 litres of water, only for a stable tank with working beneficial bacteria and plants, and only for small species.
The 1 cm per 1.5 L rule fits small community fish about 2–7 cm long and does not work for large fish.
Using the 1 cm per 1.5 L rule, a 40-litre tank holds about 26–27 cm of small fish in total length.
Ten fish of 10 g each do not equal one 100 g fish; how much a tank can carry does not depend only on total fish mass.
Ten 2 cm tetras are not the same load as one 20 cm oscar, even though their total length is equal.
Work out the tank volume by multiplying length × width × depth.
Take about 10% off the volume to allow for the space decor takes up.
Worked example: a 91 x 30 x 38 cm tank holds about 106 L, or about 96 L after the decor deduction.
Count each fish at its adult size, not the size it is when you buy it.
Before buying, look up each species' adult size, space needs and compatibility.
Let beneficial bacteria build up in the filter before adding fish; commercial bacteria products can speed this up.
Add fish in small batches over time so the bacterial colony can keep up.
Test nitrate every 2–3 weeks; only add more fish while water quality stays good and nitrate stays under 40 ppm.
In a healthy tank, ammonia and nitrite should read 0 ppm and nitrate should stay below 40 ppm.
When a tank is stocked past what it can carry, ammonia may stay high indefinitely.
Fish gasping even with aeration running is a sign of low oxygen; overcrowded fish use up oxygen quickly.
Nitrate builds up faster with more fish, more feeding or higher-protein food.
Overstocking leads to waste buildup, poor water quality, disease and death.
If fish gasp despite aeration, moving some of them to a larger tank (about 30–55 gallons) of dechlorinated water can help.
Allow for growth, use a filter with high surface area, change water regularly and test for signs of pollution.
More frequent water changes with dechlorinated water let a tank support more fish.
Fast-growing stem and floating plants absorb nitrogen compounds; more plants let the tank support more fish.
Feed only what the fish will eat, because uneaten food rots and fouls the water.
High-quality or frozen food produces less waste than cheap food.
Watch the tank over time and remove fish or trim plants if it gets crowded.
Stocking by the fishes' juvenile size: fish grow, and a tank fully stocked at once ends up heavily overstocked.
Adding more filtration without doing more maintenance; extra filtration helps but does not allow unlimited fish.
Buying many fish at once, so the filter cannot keep up.
Choosing fish by their small size in the shop without checking how big they grow.
Mixing territorial species with peaceful ones without checking compatibility.
A 91 cm tank is too small for even one adult Oscar.
Territorial fish such as cichlids need enough space to avoid fighting.
It is possible to exceed the guidelines if you know what you are doing, but the author advises against it.
Fantail goldfish grow to about 20 cm and need at least 75 litres, in a tank over 60 cm long and over 30 cm wide.
Goldfish need at least a 75-litre tank to swim comfortably.
Adult angelfish reach about 15 cm long and 18 cm tall and need a tank about 45 cm tall.
Zebra danios are only about 5 cm, but they are active and like strong current, so they need more swimming space.
Schooling species such as neon tetras and zebra danios need more room than their body size alone suggests.
Keep schooling fish in groups of about 6–10.
Pencilfish and 'bống nô lệ' clean-up fish sold young can grow to two or three times their shop size.
Oscars produce a lot of waste and leftover food.
African cichlids ('cá ali') can be stocked more densely to spread out territorial fights; add plants and hiding places to protect weaker fish.
Bettas stay near the surface and attack fish that enter their territory, so pair them with bottom- or mid-level species.
Myth: surface area is the only valid measure. Practical Fishkeeping says tanks of equal volume with equal filtration, feeding and oxygenation can hold similar numbers of fish.
Myth: a bigger filter lets you keep unlimited fish. Practical Fishkeeping says more filtration helps but needs more maintenance.
Tropical fish are comfortable at about 75–85°F and become stressed near 90°F; if water goes above about 90°F, a battery fan blowing over the open top cools it by evaporation.
During power cuts, use a battery air pump or a small generator to keep the water surface moving; don't overcrowd, because many fish use up oxygen quickly.
Before a planned outage, stop feeding a day or two ahead to cut waste; after power returns, wait 24 hours before feeding.
Larger tanks stay cooler for longer; change temperature gradually, about 1–2°F every few hours.
